title: Variables and Data Types
summary: Store values in typed variables, use const and auto, and declare, assign, and swap several variables at once.
intro: Programs need to remember things: a name, a score, a price. In C++ you store each value in a variable, and every variable has a type that the compiler checks before the program runs.

steps.title: Declaring variables
steps.body:
A variable is a named slot in memory that holds one value. C++ is statically typed: you write the type first, and the compiler fixes the variable's size and what it may hold before the program runs. Declare and initialize in one line with `type name = value;`.

```cpp
int level = 7;              // whole number
double health = 82.5;       // decimal number
char rank = 'B';            // one character, single quotes
bool online = true;         // true or false
std::string name = "Nova";  // text, needs #include <string>
```

A `char` uses single quotes and holds exactly one character. `"B"` in double quotes is a string, not a `char`. `std::string` lives in the `<string>` header, so include it whenever you use it.

Print a variable by name: `std::cout << level << '\n';` prints `7`, its value.

**Gotcha:** a `bool` prints as `1` or `0` by default. Send `std::boolalpha` to `std::cout` once and every later `bool` prints as `true` or `false`. The setting is sticky: it stays on until you turn it off with `std::noboolalpha`.

example.title: Player profile
example.prompt: Store a player's name, level, health, rank, and online flag, then print each on its own line with the flag shown as a word.
example.explanation: Each line declares a type, a name, and a starting value. `std::cout << std::boolalpha;` prints nothing. It only switches `std::cout` into word mode, so `online` prints `true` instead of `1`. `health` prints `82.5` because `std::cout` shows a `double` with up to 6 significant digits by default, and `82.5` needs only 3. `rank` prints the character `B`.

practice.title: Book record
practice.prompt:
Store a book's details in variables and print each on its own line.

1. Declare `title` as the `std::string` `"The Hobbit"`, `pages` as the `int` `310`, `price` as the `double` `12.5`, `rating` as the `char` `'A'`, and `inStock` as the `bool` `false`.
2. Turn on `std::boolalpha` so the flag prints as a word.
3. Print the five variables in that order, one per line.

Expected output:

```text
The Hobbit
310
12.5
A
false
```
hints: Write each declaration as `type name = value;`, with the `char` in single quotes.
Send `std::boolalpha` to `std::cout` before printing `inStock`, or it prints `0`.

steps.title: Changing values, const, and auto
steps.body:
Assign a new value with `=` and no type: `lives = 2;`. The new value overwrites the old one in the same slot. Writing the type again would declare a second variable with the same name, which does not compile.

Mark a value that never changes `const`. Assigning to it later is a compile error. A fixed setting such as a limit or a conversion rate is a named constant and uses UPPER_SNAKE_CASE (`MAX_LIVES`). Any other `const` value keeps a camelCase name.

```cpp
const int MAX_LIVES = 5;
auto speed = 1.5;     // auto deduces double from 1.5
int coins{10};        // brace initialization
// int bad{2.5};      // error: narrowing from double to int
```

`auto` takes the type from the initializer: `1.5` makes a `double`, `'D'` makes a `char`. Later lessons spell out simple types like `int` and `double` and save `auto` for long type names.

**Gotcha:** `auto title = "Nova";` makes a `const char*` (a pointer to raw characters), not a `std::string`. Spell out `std::string` for text.

Braces are the safer way to initialize. `int count = 2.5;` quietly drops the `.5` and stores `2`, while `int count{2.5};` stops the build so you notice. Braces only fully protect you from constants: narrowing a `double` variable, as in `int whole{price};`, just prints a warning on g++ and still compiles.

example.title: Lives counter
example.prompt: Track a player's lives as they change, next to a constant limit, an auto speed, and a brace-initialized coin count.
example.explanation: `lives` prints `3`, then each `lives = ...;` overwrites the value, so the next print shows `2` and then `5`, copied from `MAX_LIVES`. `MAX_LIVES` itself can never be reassigned. `auto` deduced `double` from `1.5`, and `coins{10}` is an ordinary `int` set with braces. The commented line shows what braces reject.

practice.title: Fuel gauge
practice.prompt:
Track a car's fuel as it changes, next to a constant tank size, an auto gear, and a brace-initialized gear count.

1. Declare `const double TANK_SIZE = 60.5;`, `int fuel = 40;`, `auto gear = 'D';`, and `int gearCount{5};`.
2. Print `fuel`, set it to `25` and print it, then set it to `55` and print it.
3. Print `TANK_SIZE`, `gear`, and `gearCount`, one per line.

Expected output:

```text
40
25
55
60.5
D
5
```
hints: `auto gear = 'D';` makes a `char`, so it prints the letter `D`.

steps.title: Several variables in one statement
steps.body:
Declare several variables of the same type in one statement by separating them with commas. Each one needs its own initializer:

```cpp
int width = 4, height = 3, depth = 2;  // all three set
```

**Gotcha:** in `int a, b = 5;` the `= 5` belongs to `b` alone. A local `int`, `double`, `char`, or `bool` without an initializer holds whatever bytes were left in that memory, and reading it is undefined behavior: the program may print anything or misbehave. Always initialize.

Print several values on one line by chaining them with a space between: `std::cout << width << ' ' << height << '\n';`.

`std::swap(a, b)` from `<utility>` exchanges two values. It parks one value in a temporary while the other moves across, so you never write that three-step dance yourself.

Chained assignment sets several variables to one value. `=` groups from right to left, so `width = height = depth = 1;` sets `depth` first, then `height`, then `width`.

C++ has no `a, b = 1, 2` form. These tools cover most needs, and structured bindings, taught in a later lesson, come closest.

example.title: Box dimensions
example.prompt: Declare three dimensions in one statement, swap two of them, then reset all three with chained assignment, printing them on one line after each change.
example.explanation: The single declaration gives each variable its own value. `std::swap(width, depth)` exchanges `4` and `2`, so the second line is `2 3 4`. `width = height = depth = 1;` assigns `1` to `depth`, that result to `height`, and that to `width`.

practice.title: Score shuffle
practice.prompt:
Declare three scores in one statement, swap two of them, then reset them all, printing them on one line after each change.

1. Declare `int first = 70, second = 85, third = 92;` in one statement and print the three values separated by single spaces.
2. Swap `first` and `third` with `std::swap` and print the three values again.
3. Set all three to `0` with one chained assignment and print them again.

Expected output:

```text
70 85 92
92 85 70
0 0 0
```
hints: Print one line with `std::cout << first << ' ' << second << ' ' << third << '\n';`.
Chained assignment looks like `first = second = third = 0;`.

recap:
- Declare with `type name = value;` using `int`, `double`, `char` (single quotes), `bool`, and `std::string` (from `<string>`).
- A `bool` prints `1` or `0` until you send `std::boolalpha`, which stays on.
- Reassign with `=` and no type. `const` values can never change.
- `auto` deduces the type from the initializer, but a string literal becomes `const char*`, not `std::string`.
- `int x{5};` is brace initialization and rejects narrowing from a constant such as `int count{2.5};`.
- `int a = 1, b = 2;` declares several at once, and each one needs its own initializer. Reading an uninitialized variable is undefined behavior.
- `std::swap` from `<utility>` exchanges two values, and `a = b = c = 0;` sets several at once.
